title: “DON’T QUESTION THE MAN OF GOD.” BUT WHAT IF GOD NEVER SAID THAT?
paragraphs: “DON’T QUESTION THE MAN OF GOD.” BUT WHAT IF GOD NEVER SAID THAT?
The sentence that has silenced wounded believers, protected unhealthy leadership, and frightened sincere Christians into confusing loyalty to a preacher with loyalty to Jesus.
Maybe you have heard it.
Maybe it was spoken from a pulpit.
Maybe it was whispered after church when someone finally gathered enough courage to ask why something did not seem biblical.
“Be careful.”
“That’s the man of God.”
“Don’t touch God’s anointed.”
“Who are you to question the pastor?”
And suddenly the conversation was over.
Not because Scripture had answered the question.
Because fear had.
That is what makes this subject so uncomfortable.

There are people reading this who genuinely love Jesus, genuinely respect spiritual leadership, genuinely do not want to gossip, rebel, slander, dishonor, or falsely accuse anyone—and yet something inside them has been troubled by what they have seen.
A teaching that did not sound like Scripture.
Money handled in ways nobody was allowed to question.
Manipulation disguised as spiritual authority.
Sin excused because the person committing it had a title.
Questions treated like rebellion.
Accountability treated like persecution.
And perhaps the most frightening part was not what happened.
It was what happened when somebody asked about it.
“Don’t question the man of God.”
But there is one question capable of cutting through generations of religious fear:
Where does the Bible actually say that?
Not church culture.
Not denominational tradition.
Not something somebody heard from somebody who heard it from a preacher thirty years ago.
Where does God’s Word teach that a Christian leader must never be questioned, examined, corrected, or held accountable?
It doesn’t.
And before anyone misunderstands what is being said, Scripture absolutely commands Christians to honor faithful spiritual leadership.
Hebrews 13:17 tells believers to obey their leaders and submit to them because those leaders keep watch over their souls and will give an account.
First Thessalonians 5:12–13 calls Christians to recognize those who labor among them and esteem them highly in love because of their work.
First Timothy 5:17 says elders who lead well are worthy of double honor, particularly those laboring in preaching and teaching.
The Bible is not anti-pastor.
It is not anti-authority.
It is not anti-church.
Jesus loves His Church.
God gives leaders to His people.
Faithful pastors, elders, teachers, missionaries, and ministry workers deserve prayer, love, respect, encouragement, and protection from malicious accusations.
But biblical honor is not biblical immunity.
Submission is not surrendering your conscience to another human being.
Respect is not pretending sin is righteousness.
And spiritual authority never places a person above the authority of Scripture.
In fact, the same Bible that commands respect for leaders commands believers to test what they hear.
Paul writes in 1 Thessalonians 5:21:
πάντα δὲ δοκιμάζετε, τὸ καλὸν κατέχετε
Panta de dokimazete, to kalon katechete.
“Test everything; hold fast what is good.”
That word δοκιμάζετε — dokimazete carries the idea of examining, testing, proving, discerning genuineness.
Notice what Paul did not say.
“Test everything except what your favorite preacher says.”
“Examine everyone except the person holding the microphone.”
“Use discernment until someone has a title.”
No.
Test everything.
That does not mean becoming cynical.
It means becoming biblical.
There is a difference.
Cynicism assumes everyone is corrupt.
Discernment asks whether something is true.
And Scripture gives us an astonishing example.
When Paul and Silas preached in Berea, Acts 17:11 says the Bereans received the word eagerly while:
ἀνακρίνοντες τὰς γραφὰς καθ᾽ ἡμέραν εἰ ἔχοι ταῦτα οὕτως
They were examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.
Think about that.
They were checking Paul.
The apostle Paul.
The man who would write a substantial portion of the New Testament.
And Luke does not condemn them for questioning whether Paul's message agreed with Scripture.
He calls them noble.
They listened eagerly...
and checked carefully.
That is biblical discernment.
A healthy spiritual leader should not be terrified when people open their Bibles.
A faithful preacher does not need Scripture kept closed to preserve his authority.
His desire should be the opposite:
“Please check what I am telling you. If I am preaching Christ faithfully, Scripture will bear witness to it. If I am wrong, Scripture outranks me.”
Because Christianity was never supposed to be built around the unquestionable personality of a preacher.
It is built upon Jesus Christ.
And Jesus does not need manipulation to remain Lord.
But then someone will quote the verse that has probably ended more church conversations than almost any other:
“Touch not mine anointed.”
Psalm 105:15.
Case closed?
Not quite.
The Hebrew reads:
אַל־תִּגְּעוּ בִמְשִׁיחָי וְלִנְבִיאַי אַל־תָּרֵעוּ
Al-tigge'u vimshichai, velinvi'ai al-tare'u.

In context, Psalm 105 is recounting God's covenant faithfulness toward the patriarchs as they wandered among nations and kingdoms. God protected His covenant people from powerful rulers who might harm them.
Read the surrounding verses.
The passage is not a blanket prohibition against asking a pastor a biblical question.
And the word often translated “touch” does not magically mean, “Never examine what a religious leader teaches.”
David's treatment of Saul makes the distinction even clearer.
David refused to murder Saul when he had opportunities to do so because Saul was the LORD's anointed king.
Yet David did not pretend Saul's behavior was righteous.
He fled from him.
He confronted him.
He publicly demonstrated Saul's wrongdoing.
He appealed to God for justice.
David refused vengeance without surrendering discernment.
That matters.
Because sometimes “honor” has been redefined to mean silence.
But silence and honor are not synonyms.
You can refuse to slander someone while still telling the truth.
You can reject vengeance while still establishing boundaries.
You can honor the office without pretending every action of the officeholder honors Christ.
You can forgive someone without calling evil good.
You can pray for a leader and still compare his teaching with Scripture.
And you can ask questions without becoming rebellious.
The New Testament goes even further.
Galatians 2 records something almost shocking when compared with modern celebrity-Christian culture.
Peter was one of the Twelve.
Peter walked with Jesus.
Peter witnessed the Transfiguration.
Peter preached at Pentecost.
Yet when Peter's conduct compromised the truth of the Gospel, Paul writes in Galatians 2:11:
Imagine someone saying to Paul:
“How dare you question Peter? He is the man of God.”
Paul's response, in effect, was that the Gospel mattered more.
That is the dividing line.
Not ego.
Not personality.
Not platform.
Not denomination.
Not popularity.
The Gospel.

Paul was so serious about this that in Galatians 1:8 he said that even if we—including himself—or even an angel from heaven preached a gospel contrary to the one already proclaimed, that messenger was to be rejected.
Paul did not create an exemption for Paul.
That is one of the marks of genuine Christian authority.
Biblical leadership points beyond itself.
False spiritual control increasingly points toward itself.
Biblical leadership says, “Follow me as I follow Christ.”
Spiritual manipulation says, “Following Christ means never questioning me.”
Those are not the same thing.
Perhaps this is where somebody's hands begin to shake a little.
Because you have lived this.
You were not trying to destroy a church.
You were trying to understand.
You did not hate your pastor.
You had a question.
You saw something.
You heard something.
You opened your Bible.
And what you found in Scripture did not seem to match what you were being told.
But instead of someone sitting beside you and opening the Word, you were made to feel dangerous.
Disloyal.
Unsubmissive.
Maybe even cursed.
So you stopped asking.
Eventually you stopped trusting your own judgment.
Maybe you even started wondering whether God was angry with you for noticing what everybody else seemed determined not to notice.
Hear this carefully.
Your conscience is not infallible.
Your interpretation is not infallible.
Your emotions are not infallible.
Your favorite online teacher is not infallible.
Your pastor is not infallible.
Neither is the person writing this article.
Scripture is the standard.
That means discernment must come with humility.
Sometimes the leader is wrong.
Sometimes we are wrong.
Sometimes what looks suspicious has a reasonable explanation.
Sometimes a disagreement is not heresy.
Sometimes a pastor makes an ordinary mistake rather than committing spiritual abuse.
Sometimes wounded people can misinterpret motives.
And sometimes critics really are divisive, dishonest, malicious, or hungry for attention.
The Bible therefore does not give Christians permission to turn “discernment” into a license for gossip.
This matters just as much.
First Timothy 5:19 warns:
“Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses.”
That protects leaders from reckless accusations.
But keep reading.
Verse 20 then deals with elders who persist in sin and says they are to be rebuked in the presence of all so that others may stand in fear.
Do you see the balance?
The Bible protects leaders from false accusation.
The Bible does not protect leaders from accountability.
That balance is beautiful.
No witch hunts.
No gossip campaigns.
No anonymous character assassination.
No weaponizing rumors because you dislike someone's preaching style.
But also...
No untouchable celebrities.
No spiritual monarchies.
No covering proven wickedness because exposing it might hurt the ministry's reputation.
No intimidating wounded people into silence by threatening them with God's judgment.
Christ's Church does not become holy by hiding scandal.
It becomes holy by walking in the light.
And this is where the story turns toward something deeper than corrupt leadership.
Because it is easy to read an article like this and think only about them.
That pastor.
That preacher.
That ministry.
That person who hurt you.
But the Gospel eventually turns the mirror around.
What about us?
Have we ever used spiritual language to protect our own pride?
Have we ever demanded grace for ourselves while demanding judgment for someone else?
Have we ever refused correction?
Have we ever hidden sin because admitting it would damage the image we built?
Have we ever wanted people to believe our reputation more than we wanted God to transform our character?
The problem of unaccountable leadership is ultimately part of a much older human problem.
We do not like being exposed.
Adam hid.
David tried to conceal what he had done.
Peter denied Jesus.
Religious leaders plotted against Christ rather than surrender their power.
And if we are honest enough, there are places inside every one of us that still whisper:
“Don't question this.”
“Don't look here.”
“Don't bring this into the light.”
Then Jesus comes.
Not merely to expose scandals.
To redeem sinners.
This is why Christianity cannot end with exposing bad pastors.
If all we do is expose hypocrisy, we may become experts at identifying darkness while never entering the light ourselves.
Jesus came for something greater.
Repentance.
Grace.
Forgiveness.
Restoration.
Transformation.
The cross announces that sin is so serious that the Son of God died for it...
and grace is so astonishing that the Son of God willingly died for sinners.
At Calvary, nobody gets to boast.
The wounded believer cannot boast.
The faithful pastor cannot boast.
The fallen pastor cannot boast.
The critic cannot boast.
The ministry founder cannot boast.
We stand on the same ground.
Sinners who need a Savior.
And that Savior has a name.
Jesus Christ.
He is the true Shepherd who never manipulates His sheep for personal glory.
He is the King whose authority is absolute because His character is perfectly holy.
He is the One who confronted religious hypocrisy while extending mercy to repentant sinners.
He is the One who washed feet.
The One who touched lepers.
The One who welcomed the broken.
The One who told the truth nobody wanted to hear.
The One who carried our sin to a Roman cross.
The One who walked out of the grave.
The One before whom every pastor, prophet, teacher, bishop, priest, apostle, ministry leader, influencer, politician, celebrity, and ordinary believer will ultimately stand.
That changes the question.
Instead of asking, “Am I allowed to question the man of God?”
Ask:
“Is everything being brought under the lordship of the Son of God?”
Because Jesus is not threatened by truth.
First John 4:1 says:
“Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God.”
Acts 5:29 gives the final boundary of human spiritual authority:
“We must obey God rather than men.”
That sentence should make abusive leadership tremble.
But it should also make rebellious hearts tremble.
Because it does not say:
“We must obey ourselves rather than men.”
It says:
God.
Our loyalty is not ultimately to our feelings.
Not to our tribe.
Not to our favorite preacher.
Not to our resentment.
Not even to our wounds.
Our loyalty belongs to God.
So yes, honor faithful pastors.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Support them.
Do not make their already difficult calling harder through gossip, suspicion, unrealistic expectations, or constant criticism.
Give grace when they make ordinary human mistakes.
Listen when mature leaders correct you.
Submit where Scripture calls you to submit.
But never turn honor into idolatry.
Never give a human being the place belonging to Christ.
And pastors, teachers, and ministry leaders who read this—please understand the extraordinary responsibility of the calling.
People may trust you with wounds they have never told their families.
They may make life decisions after hearing your sermons.
They may place enormous spiritual weight on your words.
Handle that trust with trembling hands.
Do not make disciples dependent on your personality.
Teach them to depend on Christ.
Do not become angry when they open their Bibles.
Teach them to open them wider.
Do not fear accountability.
Welcome the kind that protects both shepherd and sheep.
And when you are wrong, say the words spiritual pride hates:
“I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
Those words will not always destroy a ministry.
Sometimes they reveal that the Gospel actually lives inside it.
Because Christianity has never been the story of impressive people successfully protecting impressive reputations.
It is the story of sinners being rescued by an impressive Savior.
That is our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior.
Not because scandal does not matter.
Because Jesus can rewrite what sin tried to destroy.
Peter failed publicly—and Christ restored him.
Paul persecuted Christians—and Christ transformed him.
The thief was dying under judgment—and Christ promised him paradise.
And perhaps your story feels scandalous too.
Maybe your scandal is not public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe the thing you are hiding would shock the people who sit beside you on Sunday.
Maybe you have spent years protecting an image while your soul has been starving behind it.
Then stop hiding behind religious appearances.
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Not because repentance purchases His love, but because the Savior who loves sinners calls sinners out of darkness.
Confess your sin.
Trust in the crucified and risen Jesus.
Receive the forgiveness only He can give.
And let Him begin rewriting what you thought could never be redeemed.
Instead, be honest about your own heart.
And if Christ has restored you after spiritual hurt, consider leaving a testimony that might help somebody realize their story is not over.
Not so you can weaponize it against a pastor.
Send it to the believer who left church wounded.
Send it to the pastor who believes accountability strengthens ministry rather than threatens it.
Send it even to the skeptic who thinks Christianity requires switching off your mind.
Jesus cannot be bought, grace cannot be purchased, and salvation is never for sale.

But supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical way to help biblical content reach another exhausted believer, another wounded Christian, another seeker, another person scrolling alone at midnight wondering whether Jesus still wants them.
If you want to help Gospel Warrior keep proclaiming Christ, sharing these articles is one of the simplest things you can do.
Do not replace one religious personality with another.
Do not make Gospel Warrior your foundation.
Do not make a pastor your foundation.
Do not make an author your foundation.
Do not make a denomination your foundation.
Build on Christ.
Open your Bible.
Test what you hear.
Honor faithful leaders.
Reject malicious gossip.
Refuse spiritual intimidation.
Repent when you are wrong.
Forgive as Christ teaches you to forgive.
Protect the vulnerable.
Walk in truth.
And keep your eyes on Jesus.
Because one day every microphone will be silent.
Every platform will disappear.
Every follower count will become meaningless.
Every ministry brand will end.
Every human reputation will stand naked before eternity.
But Jesus Christ will still be King.
So perhaps the sentence Christians most desperately need is not:
“Don't question the man of God.”
Perhaps it is:
“Never become so impressed with the man of God that you stop listening to the Word of God.”
Share that with somebody before fear teaches them to confuse silence with faithfulness.
And never forget this:
Jesus does not ask you to protect darkness so His Church can look clean; He calls us into the light because His grace is strong enough to meet us there.
